clue.text: Arts quotas too complex for Italian poet

indicators.note: complex here means tangled or intricate, telling the solver to rework the preceding letters

explanation.surface: An Italian poet is bewildered by intricate arts funding quotas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' rearranges the thirteen letters of ARTS QUOTAS TOO. The answer is the sixteenth-century author of Jerusalem Delivered, also the subject of a Goethe play.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Gerusalemme Liberata is the great Italian epic poet of the Renaissance.

clue.text: Fresh German incendiaries in Swiss theatre

definitions.text: Fresh German incendiaries in Swiss theatre

parts.words: Fresh German incendiaries in Swiss theatre
parts.note: the German word for fresh is Frisch, the surname of the Swiss dramatist whose play about arsonists has this English title

explanation.walkthrough: Max Frisch's play Biedermann und die Brandstifter is known in English by this title; 'Fresh German' is a punning pointer to the playwright's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Incendiaries are arsonists, people who start blazes, which is what the play's English title calls them.

clue.text: Downfall reported by Bromfield

parts.note: Louis Bromfield's novel The ... Came, set in India, tells of the monsoon downpours

explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' sounds like ruin, but here it means water falling from the sky, as in the title of Bromfield's 1937 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy falls of water from the sky are a literal downfall, and they arrive in the title of Bromfield's monsoon novel.

clue.text: Like Wildfell Hall without Helen?

parts.note: Helen Graham is the occupant in Anne Bronte's novel The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, so without her the house has no occupant

explanation.walkthrough: Anne Bronte's heroine Helen is the tenant of the title; take her away and the hall stands empty of anyone renting it.
explanation.definitionFit: A house with no occupant renting it is vacant, which is how Wildfell Hall would be without its tenant.

clue.text: Late flu somehow reminiscent of Chaucer's work?

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters arrive in some unspecified new order

explanation.surface: A late bout of influenza somehow recalls a medieval poet's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges LATE FLU. The question mark flags a playful definition: Chaucer's best-known work is The Canterbury Tales, so something full of tales recalls it.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of stories or tales, much as Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims fill the road with storytelling.

clue.text: Virgin daughter of rumoured spurious father, in tragic rockfall

definitions.text: Virgin daughter of rumoured spurious father, in tragic rockfall

parts.words: Virgin daughter of rumoured spurious father, in tragic rockfall
parts.note: the Roman Vestal who betrayed the Capitol was the daughter of Spurius, a name that sounds like spurious, and gave her name to the rock traitors were thrown from

explanation.walkthrough: In Roman legend this Vestal virgin, daughter of Spurius Tarpeius, let the Sabines into the citadel; the Tarpeian Rock, from which traitors were hurled, bears her name.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Roman Vestal who betrayed the citadel and gave her name to the execution cliff on the Capitoline.

clue.text: His characters were bound to please

definitions.text: His characters were bound to please

parts.words: His characters were bound to please
parts.note: the eighteenth-century French marquis whose novels feature people tied up for others' gratification

explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to please' normally means sure to delight; here the characters are literally bound, in the works of the French libertine marquis.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marquis whose name gives us sadism wrote novels full of characters tied up for pleasure.

clue.text: "John was sharply ordered to dismount and -his horse" (Rider Haggard, Jess)

definitions.text: "John was sharply ordered to dismount and -his horse" (Rider Haggard, Jess)

parts.words: "John was sharply ordered to dismount and -his horse" (Rider Haggard, Jess)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Haggard's South African novel Jess, where the missing verb means to unsaddle

explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled by an old South African verb meaning to take the saddle off a horse, as used in Haggard's novel Jess.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsaddle a horse and let it rest is what the South African term describes, completing Haggard's sentence.

clue.text: Yeats sonnet for birdlover

parts.note: the Yeats sonnet about the Spartan queen ravished by Zeus in the form of a bird, so its title names a lover of a bird

explanation.walkthrough: 'birdlover' sounds like a birdwatcher, but the lover here is the mythical queen, and the bird is Zeus in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's 1924 sonnet retells the myth of Zeus as a swan with the Spartan queen, a literal bird and its lover.

clue.text: St Pauls sort of writer

parts.note: St Paul wrote letters to the early churches, the Epistles, so he is a writer of that kind

explanation.walkthrough: 'St Pauls' looks like the cathedral, but it means the apostle, author of letters to the Corinthians, Romans and others.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of letters, and specifically the reader of the Epistle in church, as St Paul was the Epistles' author.

clue.text: Chronicler of the French enemy

parts.note: de is the French word for of
a foe is an enemy

explanation.surface: Someone records the doings of France's foes.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of A Journal of the Plague Year was a chronicler of events as well as a novelist.

clue.text: His supporters may believe in ghosts

definitions.text: His supporters may believe in ghosts

parts.words: His supporters may believe in ghosts
parts.note: the Norwegian playwright's admirers think well of his play Ghosts

explanation.walkthrough: 'believe in ghosts' suggests the supernatural, but Ghosts is the Norwegian dramatist's 1881 play, which his admirers champion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian dramatist who wrote Ghosts and A Doll's House would naturally have fans who back that play.

clue.text: Parasitical element of song by modest composer

definitions.text: Parasitical element of song by modest composer

parts.words: Parasitical element of song by modest composer
parts.note: Modest Mussorgsky wrote the Song of the ..., whose subject is a biting insect

explanation.walkthrough: 'modest' looks like an adjective, but it is Mussorgsky's first name, Modest, composer of a famous song about a jumping parasite.
explanation.definitionFit: A small jumping bloodsucking insect is a parasite, and it is the subject of Mussorgsky's song.

clue.text: Where Huxley's bad vision was worse than ever?

definitions.text: Where Huxley's bad vision was worse than ever?

parts.words: Where Huxley's bad vision was worse than ever?
parts.note: Aldous Huxley, who had poor eyesight, wrote Eyeless in ..., naming the place where the blinded Samson laboured

explanation.walkthrough: Huxley's novel Eyeless in Gaza borrows Milton's line about blinded Samson; Huxley himself was nearly blind, hence 'bad vision was worse'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Philistine city where Samson was blinded supplies the title of Huxley's novel about seeing nothing.

clue.text: Amusing fellow who produced City Lights

definitions.text: Amusing fellow who produced City Lights

parts.words: Amusing fellow who produced City Lights
parts.note: City Lights is not Chaplin's film here but the memoir by the Yorkshire humorist who wrote Billy Liar

explanation.walkthrough: 'City Lights' points at Chaplin, but this is Keith's 1994 memoir of his Leeds boyhood; he was a comic novelist and columnist.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith, comic novelist and newspaper humorist, wrote the memoir City Lights, so he was an amusing writer.

clue.text: Forster's moment is now, said Tillich

definitions.text: Forster's moment is now, said Tillich

parts.words: Forster's moment is now, said Tillich
parts.note: E. M. Forster wrote The ... Moment and Paul Tillich wrote The ... Now, the same adjective serving both titles

explanation.walkthrough: One adjective completes both titles: Forster's story collection The Eternal Moment and the theologian Tillich's sermons The Eternal Now.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasting for ever, without beginning or end, describes both Forster's moment and Tillich's present.

clue.text: A word for Gypsy Rose Lee from H. L. Mencken

definitions.text: A word for Gypsy Rose Lee from H. L. Mencken

parts.words: A word for Gypsy Rose Lee from H. L. Mencken
parts.note: Mencken coined a pseudo-Greek term for a stripper, from the word for moulting, at the request of an American burlesque performer

explanation.walkthrough: Mencken invented the word in 1940 from Greek ekdysis, shedding a skin; Gypsy Rose Lee was the famous American burlesque stripper.
explanation.definitionFit: Mencken's coinage means a striptease artiste, one who sheds clothes as a snake moults, apt for Gypsy Rose Lee.

clue.text: A poor professor goes to hell

parts.note: bad means poor in quality
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: An inadequate academic ends up in the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to' is a link: the pieces simply follow one another. The answer is the Hebrew name for the bottomless pit, used by Milton.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrew word for destruction names the bottomless pit or place of the dead in Revelation and Milton.

clue.text: Warrior herald, helmeted and armoured, protects Latin poet

indicators.note: the words herald and helmeted shelter the answer, which runs across them

explanation.surface: An armoured warrior and his helmeted herald stand guard over a classical poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warrior' and 'and armoured' are surface dressing; 'protects' says the answer sits within 'herald, helmeted'. Aldhelm was a seventh-century English bishop who wrote in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon abbot of Malmesbury composed riddles and verse in Latin, so he counts as a poet in that tongue.

clue.text: Opera composer in motet version

indicators.note: a version is a new rendering, so the letters are given in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A composer of operas appears in an arrangement of a motet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version' rearranges IN MOTET; 'in' looks like a link but is part of the fodder. Gian Carlo was the Italian-American composer of Amahl and the Night Visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: Gian Carlo wrote The Medium and The Consul, both stage works, making him an opera composer.

clue.text: Gerard, Reade's merciful father

parts.note: in Reade's The Cloister and the Hearth the hero Gerard takes holy orders and a religious name meaning merciful

explanation.walkthrough: Gerard, hero of Charles Reade's novel, becomes a friar, a 'father', under a name that also means lenient.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means lenient or forgiving, and it is the name Gerard takes as a friar in Reade's novel.

clue.text: Asia, doubtless recognizable in new atlas

definitions.text: Asia, doubtless recognizable in new atlas

parts.words: Asia, doubtless recognizable in new atlas
parts.note: Asia is here an Oceanid nymph, also known by another name as the mother of the Titan who holds up the sky

explanation.walkthrough: 'Asia' and 'atlas' suggest geography, but they are mythical: the Oceanid Asia is identified with the wife of Iapetus, and Atlas is her son.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Oceanid wife of Iapetus, sometimes called Asia, is mother of Atlas and Prometheus.

clue.text: Feuchtwanger's hero is American in short story

indicators.note: in places the American abbreviation within the letters for short story

parts.note: SS is an abbreviation used for short story

explanation.surface: A German novelist's protagonist turns out to be a Yank in a brief tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link. Lion Feuchtwanger's novel Jud Suss centres on the eighteenth-century financier Joseph Suss Oppenheimer.
explanation.definitionFit: Feuchtwanger's novel Jew Suss takes its title from its protagonist, the court financier Joseph Oppenheimer.

clue.text: Like Lurie's children

parts.note: Alison Lurie wrote the novel ... Children, meaning children without siblings

explanation.walkthrough: Alison Lurie's 1979 novel is Only Children; the adjective describes children with no brothers or sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: Children with no siblings are sole offspring, as in the title of Alison Lurie's novel.

clue.text: Composer of Le Chasseur Maudit

indicators.note: of here means taken out of, the answer forming part of the French word that follows

explanation.surface: A clue asks who wrote the symphonic poem The Accursed Huntsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Chasseur Maudit is really by Cesar Franck; the answer, the German baroque opera composer Johann Adolf, sits inside the word 'Chasseur'.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Adolf was a prolific eighteenth-century German composer of opera seria.

clue.text: Where trials revealed some universal embarrassment

indicators.note: revealed some says part of the following words is laid bare as the answer

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.walkthrough: The draft read 'Where trials revealed' as the definition, which cannot stand for a place name; 'Where trials' is the definition and 'revealed some' the signal for the letters inside 'universal embarrassment'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Massachusetts town hosted the notorious witch trials of 1692.

clue.text: Olympian drinks waitress

parts.note: the goddess of youth who poured nectar for the gods on Mount Olympus

explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympian' suggests the Games, but it means a dweller on Olympus: the daughter of Zeus and Hera who served the gods their nectar.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of youth acted as cupbearer to the gods, serving their drink on Olympus.

clue.text: French writer shows ecstasy in anger

indicators.note: in places the drug's letter within the word for fury

parts.note: rage means anger
E is the slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A French author displays rapture amid fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' is a link. Pauline Reage was the pen name of the author of Story of O.
explanation.definitionFit: Pauline Reage was the pseudonym of Anne Desclos, the French author of Histoire d'O.

clue.text: Mrs Hall's man wanted

parts.note: a man who is wanted by the police is a fugitive outside the law, the title of a work associated with Mrs Hall

explanation.walkthrough: 'wanted' reads as desired, but in the sense of sought by the law it describes a fugitive.
explanation.definitionFit: A man wanted by the authorities is a fugitive, someone beyond the protection of law.

clue.text: Eliot's homily delivered to

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Eliot's homily delivered to (13)': it appears cut short after 'to' and no scan or search gives the rest
